It is the main channel through which a manager learns what is really happening and passes on know-how. He suggests asking one more question when the person seems to have finished, because the important issue often comes last. How often to meet depends on how experienced the person is in their current task.

cards.title: Match your style to readiness
cards.body: No single management style is right. Grove ties it to how experienced a person is with the specific task at hand. Someone new to a task needs precise instruction and close follow-up. As they gain skill, the manager moves to discussion and support, and later to agreeing goals and watching from a distance. A veteran given an unfamiliar job needs close guidance again. Treating everyone the same is unfair to both beginners and experts.

books.title: The Effective Executive
books.author: Peter F. Drucker
books.why: The founding text on managing oneself in knowledge work, built on the claim that effectiveness is a set of habits anyone can learn.

cards.title: Effectiveness can be learned
cards.body: Drucker observed that intelligence, imagination and knowledge are common among professionals, and yet few get the right things done. Effectiveness, he argues, is not a talent or a personality type. It is a handful of practices that can be learned as a child learns multiplication tables, through repetition. By executive he means anyone whose decisions affect results, which today includes most people whose work is thinking.

cards.title: Know where your time goes
cards.body: Drucker starts with time, not tasks, because time is the one resource that cannot be bought or stored. He asks people to record their actual time use, since memory is badly wrong about it. Then prune: drop what need not be done at all, hand on what others can do, and stop wasting other people's time. Lastly, gather what remains into large blocks, because serious work cannot be done in scattered quarter-hours.
cards.try: Keep a rough log of how you spend tomorrow, in half-hour blocks. Do not judge it yet; just record.

cards.title: Ask what you can contribute
cards.body: Most people focus on their effort and their authority. Drucker asks a different question: what can I contribute that will significantly affect the results of the organisation I serve? This turns attention outward, to the client or the person who uses your output. A developer who asks it stops thinking in terms of tickets closed and starts thinking about whether the client's customers can now do what they needed to do.

cards.title: Build on strength
cards.body: Results come from using strengths, not from repairing weaknesses. Drucker applies this to staffing, where he advises choosing a person for what they do exceptionally well and accepting the flaws that come with it. He applies it to managing your boss, by learning how they work best. And he applies it to yourself: know your strong areas and the way you work, and arrange your tasks to use them. Trying to be good at everything produces mediocrity.

cards.title: First things first, one at a time
cards.body: Drucker's secret of effectiveness is concentration: do the most important thing first and do only one thing at a time. That requires courage as much as analysis, because it means saying no to other worthy things. He adds a regular discipline of abandonment. Review existing activities and ask, if we were not already doing this, would we start it now? If the answer is no, stop. Old commitments crowd out new opportunities.
cards.try: Look at your recurring commitments and ask of one: if I were not already doing this, would I start it now?

cards.title: Few decisions, made well
cards.body: Effective people, in Drucker's account, do not make many decisions. They make a few important ones and take time over them. They first ask whether a problem is a one-off or a sign of something general that needs a rule. They seek out disagreement, since a decision nobody argued against has not been examined. And a decision is not complete until someone is named to carry it out and the steps are clear.

books.title: Radical Candor
books.author: Kim Scott
books.why: A simple, memorable framework for giving honest feedback without being either cruel or uselessly nice.

cards.title: Care and challenge together
cards.body: Scott's model has two axes: how much you care about the person, and how willing you are to challenge them directly. Good feedback needs both. Caring without challenging leaves people uninformed; challenging without caring makes them defensive. When someone knows you are on their side, they can hear hard things from you. The framework describes behaviour in a given moment, not a type of person; everyone slides between the four corners.

cards.title: The kindness that harms
cards.body: The most common failure, Scott says, is staying silent to spare someone's feelings. You see a colleague's work falling short and say nothing, or soften it until the message is lost. It feels kind and it is not, because the person never gets the chance to improve and may later be surprised by a poor review or the loss of their job. Withholding the truth protects your own comfort at the other person's expense.

cards.title: Two other failures
cards.body: Challenging without care produces harsh criticism that humiliates, which Scott notes is at least clear enough to act on. Worst is neither caring nor challenging: insincere praise to someone's face and criticism behind their back, in order to be liked or to gain advantage. Naming these patterns helps you catch yourself. When you are about to stay quiet or speak, ask which of the four corners you are in.

cards.title: Ask before you give
cards.body: To build a culture of honest feedback, Scott advises starting by asking for criticism of yourself, especially if you are the boss. Ask a real question, tolerate the uncomfortable silence that follows, listen without defending yourself and then act visibly on what you heard. People will not believe you want honesty until they see someone give it and be thanked. Only then have you earned the right to give it freely.
cards.try: Ask one colleague or client: what is one thing I could do differently that would make working with me easier?

cards.title: Make it specific and quick
cards.body: Feedback works best soon after the event, in person where possible, and about the work rather than the person's character. Describe the situation, what they did and its effect, for praise as well as criticism. Vague praise such as good job teaches nothing. Criticism is best given in private and praise in public, though some people dislike public praise, so it pays to know the person.
cards.try: Give one piece of specific praise today: what the person did and what it made possible.

cards.title: Steady performers and fast climbers
cards.body: Scott distinguishes two kinds of excellent performer. Some are on a steep path, wanting new challenges and promotion. Others do excellent work and want stability in a role they are good at, perhaps because of what else is going on in their lives. Teams need both, and people move between the two over a career. Managers err by pushing everyone towards promotion, or by ignoring steady people who hold the team together.

books.title: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team
books.author: Patrick Lencioni
books.why: A short business fable with a clear model of why capable people often fail to work as a team.

cards.title: A pyramid of problems
cards.body: Lencioni tells the story of a new chief executive taking over a talented and divided leadership team, and from it draws a model of five problems stacked like a pyramid. Each one rests on the one beneath: without trust there is no honest debate, without debate no real commitment, without commitment no accountability, and without accountability nobody attends to shared results. The model is drawn from his consulting experience, not from formal research, and is best used as a diagnostic.

cards.title: Trust means being open
cards.body: The foundation is a particular kind of trust: confidence that teammates mean well, so that there is no need to be guarded. In practice this means people can say I was wrong, I need help, or you are better at this than I am, without fear that it will be used against them. Where that is missing, energy goes into self-protection and appearances. Leaders build it by going first and admitting their own mistakes.
cards.try: In your next team conversation, admit one thing you got wrong or do not know.

cards.title: Conflict about ideas is healthy
cards.body: Teams lacking trust avoid disagreement and hold polite, dull meetings, while the real arguments happen in corridors and private messages. Lencioni argues that open, even heated, debate about ideas is necessary for good decisions, provided it stays on the issue and off the person. A meeting where nobody disagrees is a warning sign. The leader may need to draw out disagreement and then resist the urge to smooth it over.

cards.title: Commitment needs to be heard
cards.body: People can support a decision they argued against, as long as they were truly heard. Lencioni separates commitment from consensus: waiting for everyone to agree produces delay and watered-down choices. What is needed is clarity about what was decided, and willingness to act on it. He suggests ending each meeting by restating the decisions and agreeing on what will be told to others, so nobody leaves with a different version.
cards.try: End your next meeting by saying aloud what was decided and who will do what.

cards.title: Peers hold each other to account
cards.body: In strong teams, members call out each other's lapses directly, without leaving it all to the boss. This is uncomfortable, so most people avoid it, and standards slip. It is only possible when goals and responsibilities are clear and public, since nobody can be held to a vague commitment. Pressure from peers who respect each other is more effective than any rule imposed from above.

cards.title: Results before status
cards.body: At the top of the pyramid is the tendency of people to care more about their own standing, their department or their career than about the team's shared goal. A team can be full of individually successful people and still fail. The remedy is to make collective results explicit and visible, and to recognise people for what the team achieves. If the group fails, nobody has succeeded, however good their own figures look.

books.title: The Goal
books.author: Eliyahu M. Goldratt and Jeff Cox
books.why: A novel about saving a factory that teaches how to find the one constraint limiting any system, including a team or a one-person business.

cards.title: Be clear on the goal
cards.body: A plant manager facing closure is asked by an old teacher what the goal of his company is. After some false starts he concludes that it is to make money, and that things like efficiency or new technology count only as far as they serve that. The book reduces measurement to three questions: how much money comes in through sales, how much is tied up inside the system, and how much is spent running it.

cards.title: Every system has a bottleneck
cards.body: The output of any process is set by its slowest step. Goldratt illustrates this with a line of boys on a hike: the group moves at the pace of the slowest walker, however fast the others go, and gaps open up ahead of him. In a factory it is one overloaded machine; in a web agency it may be the single person who approves designs. Speeding up any other step changes nothing about how much gets finished.

cards.title: An hour lost at the bottleneck
cards.body: Since the bottleneck sets the pace of the whole system, an hour it sits idle is an hour of output lost for the entire operation. An hour saved anywhere else is worthless. So the first move is to squeeze the most from the constraint as it is: never let it wait for work, never let it work on things that are not needed, and check quality before work reaches it so its time is not spent on faulty input.

cards.title: Busy is not productive
cards.body: The story's most surprising claim is that keeping every person and machine fully occupied is harmful. If steps before the bottleneck work at full speed, they simply build piles of half-finished work that the bottleneck cannot absorb. That ties up money and hides problems. Non-bottleneck resources should work at the bottleneck's pace and sometimes stand idle. Being idle at the right time is correct, a hard idea in a culture that rewards looking busy.

cards.title: Five steps, then repeat
cards.body: Goldratt turns the story into a method. Identify the constraint. Decide how to get the most from it as it is. Make everything else follow its pace. Only then spend money to increase its capacity. When it is no longer the limit, go back and find the new one, because there always is one. The warning is against inertia: rules made for the old constraint can quietly become the new problem.
cards.try: Ask of your own work: where do tasks pile up waiting? That step, not the busiest one, is your constraint.

books.title: The E-Myth Revisited
books.author: Michael E. Gerber
books.why: Explains why skilled people struggle when they start a business around their skill, and what to build instead of a job for yourself.

cards.title: The myth in the title
cards.body: Gerber's E-Myth is the belief that small businesses are started by entrepreneurs. Most, he says, are started by technicians: people good at a craft, such as baking, repairing or coding, who are tired of working for someone else. They assume that knowing how to do the work means knowing how to run a business that does that work. These are different skills, and the confusion explains why so many capable people end up exhausted by their own firms.

cards.title: Three people in one owner
cards.body: Each owner, Gerber says, has three characters inside. The technician wants to do the work, now. The manager wants order, planning and systems. The entrepreneur looks ahead and imagines what the business could become. In most small owners the technician dominates, so the business gets plenty of doing and little planning or vision. A healthy business needs all three, even when they are the same person on different days.
cards.try: Look at last week: roughly how many hours went to doing client work, to organising, and to thinking about where the business is going?

cards.title: Work on it, not only in it
cards.body: A technician-run business depends wholly on its owner. If you do not work, there is no income; you have built yourself a job with a demanding boss. Gerber urges owners to step back regularly and work on the business itself: how it finds customers, delivers, charges and could run without them in each role. Even one protected hour a week of this changes the direction, because otherwise urgent client work always wins.

cards.title: Build it like a model to copy
cards.body: Gerber asks owners to imagine their business as the pattern for many identical branches, the way successful franchises are designed, even if they never intend to open a second one. The exercise forces useful questions. Could a newly trained person deliver the same result every time? Is the way you work written down anywhere? A business that gives a consistent experience, regardless of who is on duty, is one customers can trust.

cards.title: Systems first, people within them
cards.body: In Gerber's view the consistency of a business should come from documented ways of working, with people operating those systems, and not from exceptional individuals. A checklist for launching a client's site, a standard way of answering enquiries and a script for taking on a new client mean that quality does not hinge on anyone's memory. Critics find this too mechanical for creative work, but even there routine parts can be systematised to free attention for the rest.
cards.try: Write down the steps of one task you repeat for clients, as if for someone doing it for the first time.

cards.title: Three phases of growth
cards.body: Gerber describes a business as moving through stages. In infancy the owner does everything, and the business is the owner. In adolescence the owner hires help and tends to hand work over without guidance, then takes it back when quality drops, returning to overwork. Maturity is a business built on purpose from the start, with a clear picture of how it should operate when finished. Most small firms get stuck in the first two.

books.title: The Lean Startup
books.author: Eric Ries
books.why: Sets out the now-standard method for testing a business idea quickly and cheaply before betting everything on it.

cards.title: Learning is the unit of progress
cards.body: A start-up, in Ries's definition, is any venture creating something new under great uncertainty. Its real output early on is not features or revenue but knowledge of what customers actually want. Building a polished product nobody uses is waste, however efficiently it was built. So he measures progress by validated learning: things you have shown to be true by experiment with real customers, as opposed to things you believe.

cards.title: Build, measure, learn
cards.body: Ries describes a loop. Turn an idea into something customers can use, measure how they respond, and learn whether your assumption held. Then go round again. The aim is to shorten the time for one full loop, since a team that completes ten cycles learns more than a team that completes one. Planning runs in reverse order: decide what you need to learn, then what to measure, then the least you can build to get that measurement.

cards.title: The smallest useful test
cards.body: A minimum viable product is the simplest version that lets you test your riskiest assumption with real people. It might be a single landing page describing a service, to see whether anyone signs up, or a service delivered by hand behind a simple form before any automation exists. It is not a shoddy product; it is an experiment. The usual error is building far more than the question requires, out of fear of looking unfinished.
cards.try: Name the riskiest assumption behind something you want to build, and the cheapest way to test it this week.

cards.title: Numbers that flatter
cards.body: Ries warns against vanity metrics, figures that tend to rise whatever you do and feel good, such as total sign-ups or page views. They do not tell you whether a change helped. Actionable metrics link cause and effect: of the people who saw the new page, what share bought, compared with the old page? He favours comparing groups of users who started at different times, and split tests, so that results cannot be explained away.
cards.try: Pick one number you track and ask whether it could ever tell you that a change made things worse.

cards.title: Pivot or persevere
cards.body: When experiments show the main assumption is wrong, the team must decide whether to keep going or to change strategy while keeping what it has learned. Ries calls the change a pivot. It might mean a different customer, a different problem or a different way of earning. He suggests regular meetings where this question is asked honestly, because teams drift for years on a failing idea when nobody is obliged to face the evidence.

cards.title: Small batches
cards.body: Borrowing from lean manufacturing, Ries argues for working in small batches: finish and release one small thing before starting the next. Large batches feel efficient and hide problems until the end, when they are costly to fix. Small ones bring errors to light at once. The method has critics, who note that some products cannot be tested in pieces and that customers cannot always tell you what they will want. It suits situations where trying things is cheap.

books.title: Rework
books.author: Jason Fried and David Heinemeier Hansson
books.why: Blunt, short essays from the founders of a small software company that question most of the usual advice about business.

cards.title: Plans are guesses
cards.body: The authors argue that long-term business plans are guesses about a future nobody can see, and that writing them down lends false confidence. Once a plan exists people follow it even when the facts change. They prefer to decide what to do this week, with the information available now, and improvise from there. This does not mean having no direction. It means holding forecasts lightly and making decisions as late as you responsibly can.

cards.title: Embrace constraints
cards.body: Having little time, money or staff is usually treated as a handicap. The authors treat it as an advantage, because limits force you to decide what really matters and to find simple solutions. A team with no budget cannot build ten features, so it builds the two that count. They built their own product while doing client work, with part-time hours. If you wait for ideal conditions, you wait forever.

cards.title: Half a product, done well
cards.body: When there is too much to do, the tempting response is to do all of it thinly. The authors recommend cutting scope in half and doing the remaining half properly. A product with fewer things that work well beats one with many things done poorly. This requires saying no to good ideas, including customers' requests, since each addition has a cost that continues long after it ships.
cards.try: Take your current to-do list for a project and mark the half that could be dropped without the client being worse off.

cards.title: Meetings and interruptions
cards.body: The authors regard interruptions as the chief enemy of getting work done. A day of meetings, calls and quick questions leaves no long stretch in which real work can happen. They point out that a one-hour meeting with ten people costs ten hours of work. Their advice: fewer meetings, with a set end time, a specific problem and as few people as possible, and a preference for messages that can be answered when convenient.

cards.title: Long hours are not a virtue
cards.body: The book criticises the culture that admires overwork. Working late is often a substitute for thinking: it hides poor decisions, creates crises and wears people out, and tired people decide badly. The person who goes home on time may have found the quicker way. The authors want the work itself to be judged, not the hours on display. A small business run on the owner's exhaustion has not solved its problem, only put it off.

cards.title: Teach instead of advertise
cards.body: A small firm cannot outspend large competitors on marketing, but it can out-teach them. Sharing what you know, through articles, guides and honest accounts of how you work, builds trust with exactly the people who may hire you. Large companies tend to be too secretive or too slow to do this. A caveat on the book overall: it reflects one profitable, self-funded software company's experience, and its confident rules will not fit every business.

books.title: The Mom Test
books.author: Rob Fitzpatrick
books.why: A brief, practical guide to asking customers questions that produce truth, not polite encouragement.

cards.title: Why your mother lies to you
cards.body: Ask your mother whether your business idea is good and she will say yes, because she loves you. Fitzpatrick's point is that almost everyone does the same out of politeness. As soon as people know what answer you hope for, they give it. So the fault lies with the question, not with them. A good question is one that even your mother could not answer with a comforting lie, because it never reveals what you are hoping to hear.

cards.title: Their life, not your idea
cards.body: The first rule is to talk about the other person's life and problems, not your product. Do not ask whether they would use an app that does a certain thing. Ask how they handle that task today, what is annoying about it and what they have tried. You learn whether the problem is real and how much it matters without describing your solution at all, so nothing is said out of kindness.

cards.title: The past, not the future
cards.body: People are poor at predicting their own behaviour and generous with promises. Would you pay for this, and would you use it, are questions that yield hopeful fiction. Ask about specific things that already happened: when did this last come up, what did you do, what did it cost you? Someone who has already spent money or effort trying to solve a problem has shown that it matters. Someone who has never even searched for a solution probably will not buy yours.
cards.try: Next time you explore a new service, ask a prospect: when did you last have this problem, and what did you do about it?

cards.title: Three kinds of bad data
cards.body: Fitzpatrick names three things that feel like progress and are not. Compliments, such as that sounds great, tell you nothing. Fluff is general or hypothetical talk, like I usually or I would. Feature ideas are requests that should be understood, not simply obeyed: ask why they want it and what it would let them do. When you hear any of these, steer back gently to specific facts about what the person really does.

cards.title: Look for commitment
cards.body: A meeting that ends with good luck, keep me posted has failed, however pleasant it was. A real signal is when the person gives up something they value: time for a further meeting, an introduction to their boss or a colleague, or money through a deposit or advance order. Fitzpatrick advises always pushing for a clear next step. If they refuse it, you have learned something true, and that is better than warm words.
cards.try: At the end of your next conversation with a prospect, ask for one concrete next step with a date.

cards.title: Keep it casual, and listen
cards.body: These conversations work best as ordinary chats, not formal interviews. A short talk at an event or at the end of a client call often reveals more than a scheduled meeting where everyone is on best behaviour. Know beforehand the few things you most need to learn, speak much less than the other person and resist pitching. The moment you begin selling, you stop learning.

books.title: The Win Without Pitching Manifesto
books.author: Blair Enns
books.why: Twelve principles for creative and consulting firms on being hired as a trusted expert, not auditioned as an interchangeable supplier.

cards.title: Specialise
cards.body: Enns's first principle is that a firm must choose a narrow focus. A generalist who builds any website for anyone is easily replaced, so the client holds the power and price decides. An expert in a clear niche, such as sites for clinics or shops built on one platform, has few real substitutes and deeper knowledge. Specialising feels risky, since it means turning work away, but it is what lets you stop competing with everyone on price.
cards.try: Finish this sentence in ten words or fewer: we help this kind of client with this kind of problem.

cards.title: Stop giving ideas away
cards.body: The traditional pitch asks firms to produce designs or strategy for free in the hope of winning the job. Enns argues this gives away the most valuable part of the work and casts you as a supplicant. He would replace the performance with a conversation between equals about whether there is a fit. Thinking is the product, and it should start when the engagement starts. A client who insists on free work first may not be the right client.

cards.title: Diagnose before you prescribe
cards.body: A doctor who prescribed without examining the patient would be negligent. Enns holds designers and consultants to the same standard. Clients often arrive with their own diagnosis, such as we need a new website, when the real issue may be something else. The expert's task is to insist politely on understanding the problem first, and to charge for that work if it is substantial. Accepting the client's diagnosis unchecked makes you an order-taker.

cards.title: Selling as helping
cards.body: Many creative people dislike selling because they picture it as persuading someone to buy what they do not need. Enns reframes it. With someone who has not yet recognised a problem, the job is to help them see it. With someone who is interested, it is to give information that helps them decide. With someone ready to buy, it is to reassure. None of that is manipulation. You are helping a person through a decision, and no is an acceptable result.

cards.title: Talk about money early
cards.body: Enns advises raising the budget near the start of the conversation, before much time is invested by either side. It is awkward, and it saves everyone from weeks of talks that end when a price is finally named. He suggests stating a minimum level of engagement so that poor fits remove themselves. Being able to discuss money plainly and without embarrassment is itself a mark of a professional.
cards.try: Decide the smallest project fee you will accept, so you can state it calmly when asked.

cards.title: Be willing to walk away
cards.body: Several of the principles come to the same thing: be selective, do not work at a loss, and charge enough to do the work properly. A firm that needs every job cannot negotiate and ends up with clients who do not respect it. The freedom to say no comes from a specialism, a steady flow of enquiries and some savings. Enns writes for established firms; someone just starting may need to compromise, and he would see that as a stage to grow out of.

books.title: Design Is a Job
books.author: Mike Monteiro
books.why: A frank guide to the business side of client work: finding clients, pricing, contracts, presenting and getting paid.

cards.title: The business is part of the craft
cards.body: Monteiro's premise is that doing good work is only half of a design career. The other half is finding clients, agreeing terms, presenting, handling feedback and collecting payment. People who see these as distractions from the real work tend to get mistreated. He treats them as professional skills to learn like any other. Explaining and selling your work is not beneath a designer or a developer; it is how good work reaches the world.

cards.title: Choose clients carefully
cards.body: Taking any client who shows up leads to bad projects. Monteiro advises judging clients as carefully as they judge you. Do they have a real problem you can solve, the authority to make decisions, and respect for what you do? Warning signs include vagueness about budget, a string of previous designers and decisions made by a large committee. Most good clients come by referral from past clients, which is one more reason to finish every project well.

cards.title: Price for value
cards.body: Monteiro suggests the price of work should reflect its value to the client and not merely the hours spent. A site that will bring a business substantial new revenue is worth more than the time it took to make. Charging too little also signals low value and attracts clients who will treat you accordingly. He advises stating your price with confidence and not negotiating against yourself by cutting it before anyone has objected.

cards.title: Always have a contract
cards.body: A contract is not a sign of distrust. It records what both sides have agreed to do, while everyone is still friendly, and so protects both. Monteiro insists on one for every job, with clear terms on scope, payment schedule, who owns the work and what happens if the project is cancelled. He recommends having a lawyer draft or review it, since contract law differs by country. Starting work before it is signed gives away your leverage.
cards.try: Check whether your current client work is covered by a signed agreement stating scope and payment terms.

cards.title: Present your own work
cards.body: Never send a design or a build off with a note asking what the client thinks. Monteiro says the person who made the work should present it, explaining how each decision serves the goals the client set. Without that guidance, clients respond with personal taste. He recommends asking for feedback on whether the work solves the problem, not on whether they like it, and treating their answers as information about a concern rather than as instructions.
cards.try: Next time you send work to a client, include three lines on how it meets the goals they gave you.

cards.title: Getting paid
cards.body: Payment problems are best prevented before work begins. Monteiro's practices include taking part of the fee up front, tying further payments to dates or milestones in the contract, and not handing over final files until the last invoice is settled. Send invoices promptly and follow up on late ones without embarrassment; you are asking for what was agreed. A client who avoids discussing payment at the start will rarely be easier at the end.
